meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Exam 2 set 2: 20 new questions per chapter and skill. Harder items, CJMM application style, 15% non multiple choice per section. No daily set flags. Each section also has 5 questions marked "difficulty": "difficult" (ids ending hd01 to hd05), placed last.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old slipped to the floor. The nurse stayed, called for help, found no injury and stable vital signs, then assisted her back to bed. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Complete the occurrence report
options.rationale: Required, and tempting because it feels urgent. It comes after the provider knows about the fall.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: The assessment is done. The provider must be told so hidden injury can be evaluated and orders written.

options.text: Reassess her for injury a second time
options.rationale: The stem already gives a complete assessment with no change since.

options.text: Hold the post-fall huddle with the team
options.rationale: Valuable for prevention, and it waits until the client's immediate care is finished.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: call for help, stay, assess, notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the plan, then document and report.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you assessment is finished. Find the next step in the sequence instead of assessing again.

steps.detail: Help called, nurse stayed, injury assessed.
Nothing new has happened to assess.

steps.action: Rank the paperwork and the huddle
steps.detail: Both follow provider notification.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider. Assessment is complete, so communication is due.

questions.stem: A confused 84-year-old kept pulling at his feeding tube. The nurse taped the tube out of sight and asked his daughter to sit with him. Which finding indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: He is asleep 20 minutes after a dose of lorazepam
options.rationale: A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint, so this does not show the alternatives worked.

options.text: His hands are resting quietly inside secured mitts
options.rationale: Mitts are a restraint. Quiet hands in mitts say nothing about the alternatives.

options.text: He has left the tube alone for four hours while awake
options.rationale: The goal behavior is met without any restriction, during the time he was able to pull.

options.text: His daughter says he seems more like himself today
options.rationale: Encouraging, and it is an impression. The tube staying untouched is the measured outcome.

questions.takeaway: Judge a restraint alternative by the target behavior stopping while the client is free and awake.
questions.strategy: Ask what the plan was meant to change. Then pick the finding that shows that change without a restraint doing the work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tube left in place with no restraint.

steps.action: Remove options where something else did the work
steps.detail: Lorazepam and mitts are restraints.
An awake client leaving the tube alone beats a general impression.

elimination.verdict: Tube untouched for four hours while awake.

questions.stem: A post-fall huddle reviews a 0300 fall. The bed was low, the call light was in reach and nonslip socks were on. Zolpidem was started that evening. Which factor most likely contributed?

options.text: An unsafe room environment
options.rationale: The stem shows the environmental precautions were in place.

options.text: Missing universal fall precautions
options.rationale: Low bed, call light and footwear were all present.

options.text: Lack of an assistive device
options.rationale: Nothing in the review suggests she needed or lacked a device.

options.text: An effect of the new medication
options.rationale: A new sedative is the one thing that changed, and it impairs balance and alertness at night.

questions.takeaway: In a huddle, ask what happened, what contributed and whether interventions were in place. When precautions were in place, look for what is new.
questions.strategy: Cross off each factor the stem shows was covered. What remains is the change made that evening.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bed, call light and footwear were correct.
Zolpidem started that evening.
A 0300 fall fits a bedtime sedative.

elimination.verdict: The new medication.

questions.stem: A client receiving maintenance IV fluid says his hand tingles each time he touches the infusion pump. The nurse sees a frayed power cord. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Unplug the pump and take it out of use
options.rationale: Tingling means current is leaking. Removing the source protects the client before anything else, and maintenance fluid can pause briefly.

options.text: Call clinical engineering to inspect the pump
options.rationale: Needed, and tempting. It leaves the client touching a faulty device while you wait.

options.text: Wrap the frayed section with tape
options.rationale: A repair by the nurse does not make the device safe to use.

options.text: Assess the hand for burns and sensation
options.rationale: Reasonable after the hazard is gone. The cue already tells you the pump is the problem.

questions.takeaway: Faulty electrical equipment is unplugged and removed from service first, then tagged and reported.
questions.strategy: The tingling plus the frayed cord is the assessment. Remove the hazard before you report it or examine the hand.

steps.detail: Tingling plus frayed cord means electrical leak.
Tape does not fix a damaged cord.
Remove the source, then assess the hand, then call engineering.

elimination.verdict: Unplug and remove the pump first.

questions.stem: After report, the nurse has four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: A client in wrist restraints who reports numb, tingling fingers
options.rationale: An actual neurovascular change from the restraint. It needs a nurse's assessment and release now.

options.text: A high fall risk client asking for help to the bathroom
options.rationale: Urgent and tempting. Assistive personnel can assist with toileting right away, so it does not need the nurse first.

options.text: A client whose restraint order expires in one hour
options.rationale: Needs reassessment within the hour, and nothing is wrong yet.

options.text: A client stable after a fall, waiting for a hip x-ray
options.rationale: Already assessed and stable.

questions.takeaway: Actual harm outranks potential harm. A need that can be delegated does not have to take the nurse's first visit.
questions.strategy: Two clients cannot wait. Ask which one needs the nurse's own judgment and which one can be met by assistive personnel.

steps.detail: The x-ray client and the expiring order can wait.
Numb fingers are actual injury. The bathroom trip is a risk.
Toileting help goes to assistive personnel now.

elimination.verdict: The restrained client with numb, tingling fingers.

questions.stem: An alert 68-year-old who reliably uses the call light became dizzy on standing after starting a new blood pressure medication. Which intervention should the nurse add to the plan?

options.text: Keep her on bed rest until the dizziness stops
options.rationale: Immobility adds weakness. The goal is safe mobility.

options.text: Turn on the bed exit alarm
options.rationale: Tempting for any fall risk. An alarm targets clients who get up without calling, and she calls reliably.

options.text: Schedule toileting every one to two hours
options.rationale: Targets urgency, which she does not have.

options.text: Have her sit at the bedside before standing with assistance
options.rationale: Targets the actual risk, dizziness on standing, and keeps her moving.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the risk factor. Medication dizziness gets symptom monitoring, timing changes and assisted, gradual position change.
questions.strategy: Each option is a real fall measure. Only one matches dizziness on standing in a client who calls for help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Medication dizziness with position change.
Toileting schedule fits urgency. Bed rest causes weakness.
She already calls, so an alarm adds nothing.

elimination.verdict: Sit at the bedside first, then stand with help.

questions.stem: A client receiving oxygen by nasal cannula is in bed when a wastebasket in the room catches fire. The client cannot walk alone. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Close the room door and shut off the oxygen supply
options.rationale: Third. Confining the fire and removing oxygen slows its spread.

options.text: Move the client out of the room
options.rationale: First. This client is in immediate danger and cannot leave alone.

options.text: Use the extinguisher if the fire is still small
options.rationale: Last, and only if it can be done safely.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm
options.rationale: Second. Help is called once the client is out of danger.

questions.takeaway: RACE with a client in the room: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. Oxygen is shut off as part of confining the fire.
questions.strategy: Compare with a fire where no one is in danger. Here the client is beside the fire and cannot walk, so rescue applies.

steps.detail: The client is in the room and dependent.
The alarm brings help while you confine.
Only for a small fire with an exit behind you.

elimination.verdict: Rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish.

questions.stem: A nurse taught the wife of a client with new seizures what to do at home. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I will hold his arms so he cannot hit anything."
options.rationale: Restraining during a seizure causes injury.

options.text: "I will turn him on his side and time it."
options.rationale: Side lying protects the airway, and timing tells her when emergency help is needed.

options.text: "I will get him back into bed right away."
options.rationale: Sounds protective. He is not moved during the seizure. She clears the area around him instead.

options.text: "I will slide a soft cloth between his teeth."
options.rationale: Nothing goes in the mouth during a seizure.

questions.takeaway: During a seizure: stay, time it, protect the head, turn to the side, clear the area. Do not restrain, move or put anything in the mouth.
questions.strategy: Sort the statements into protecting him and controlling him. The correct one protects without forcing anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Holding arms and lifting to bed.
The cloth.
Side lying and a watch.

elimination.verdict: Turn him on his side and time it.

questions.stem: A confused client keeps picking at her IV dressing but is calm and stays in bed. Which measure should the nurse try first?

options.text: Request an order for soft wrist restraints
options.rationale: The most restrictive choice here, and alternatives have not been tried.

options.text: Request a dose of lorazepam at bedtime
options.rationale: A drug used to control behavior is a chemical restraint.

options.text: Apply hand mitts secured at the wrists
options.rationale: Less restrictive than wrist restraints, so it tempts. It is still a restraint, and a non-restraint option remains.

options.text: Cover the site with a sleeve and give her something to hold
options.rationale: Hides the stimulus and occupies her hands without restricting movement.

questions.takeaway: Try environmental changes and diversion before any restraint. Least restrictive means no restraint when that will work.
questions.strategy: Rank the options from most to least restrictive. Her behavior is mild, so start at the bottom of the list.

steps.detail: Picking, calm, staying in bed.
Wrist ties, mitts and sedation all restrict.
Out of sight plus a diversion.

elimination.verdict: Cover the site and give a diversion.

questions.stem: A nurse sees small flames in a linen cart in the hallway. The nearby clients are in their rooms with doors closed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Move the nearest clients to another wing
options.rationale: Rescue comes first only when someone is in immediate danger. These clients are behind closed doors.

options.text: Close the remaining open doors on the unit
options.rationale: Confining follows the alarm.

options.text: Activate the fire alarm
options.rationale: No one needs rescue, so the next step is to get help coming.

options.text: Get the extinguisher and put out the flames
options.rationale: Tempting because the fire is small. Fighting it alone before the alarm risks losing control with no help on the way.

questions.takeaway: RACE: rescue, alarm, confine, extinguish. When no one is in immediate danger, the alarm is the first action.
questions.strategy: Check whether the rescue step applies. The closed doors tell you it does not, so move to the next letter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No client is near the flames.
It is the last step.
Alarm, then confine.

elimination.verdict: Activate the alarm.

questions.stem: A client weak after a long illness has a fall plan that includes assisted walking. Which finding at the end of the shift indicates the plan is working?

options.text: She walked to the bathroom three times with a gait belt and assistance
options.rationale: Safe movement and maintained strength are the stated goals for weakness.

options.text: She stayed in bed all shift and had no falls
options.rationale: No fall, and tempting. Immobility worsens her weakness and raises tomorrow's risk.

options.text: She walked to the bathroom alone without calling
options.rationale: Unassisted walking in a weak client is the behavior the plan is meant to prevent.

options.text: She says she is afraid to get up without the nurse
options.rationale: Fear that limits movement shows lost confidence.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention is safe mobility. Success is movement with the right help, and a shift in bed is not success.
questions.strategy: Do not count only falls. Ask which finding shows she moved and moved safely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safe movement and strength.
In bed all shift versus walking with help.

steps.action: Cut the unsafe and the fearful
steps.detail: Walking alone and refusing to move.

elimination.verdict: Three assisted walks with a gait belt.

questions.scenario: A client has had bilateral soft wrist restraints for 2 hours after pulling out a central line. The nurse releases one wrist at a time for the scheduled check.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it shows the restraint care is effective or requires the nurse to act.

rows.text: Fingers warm with brisk capillary refill
rows.rationale: Circulation is intact below the cuff.

rows.text: Reddened skin under the left cuff that does not blanch
rows.rationale: Early skin injury. The cuff needs padding or repositioning and the need is reassessed.

rows.text: Moves each wrist and elbow through full range when released
rows.rationale: Mobility is being maintained.

rows.text: Last offered fluids and the urinal 4 hours ago
rows.rationale: Hydration and elimination needs are overdue for a client who cannot meet them alone.

rows.text: More agitated and straining against the cuffs than at application
rows.rationale: Increased agitation is a restraint complication and raises the risk of injury from escape attempts.

rows.text: Calm, follows directions and leaves the new line alone during release
rows.rationale: The reason for the restraint is gone, so the nurse acts to have it removed as early as possible.

questions.takeaway: Each restraint check covers skin, circulation, range of motion, hydration, elimination, comfort and mental status, and asks whether the restraint is still needed.
questions.strategy: A good finding can still require action. A calm client who leaves the line alone means the restraint should come off.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warm fingers and full range are fine. Nonblanching redness is injury.
Four hours without fluids or toileting is overdue.

steps.action: Check the need for the restraint
steps.detail: Worse agitation and a calm cooperative client both call for a change.

elimination.verdict: Effective, action, effective, action, action, action.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews how assistive personnel secured a client's wrist restraint. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The strap is tied to the raised side rail
options.rationale: Moving the rail pulls the limb and can injure the client. Straps go on the bed frame.

options.text: The strap is secured with a quick-release tie
options.rationale: Correct. It allows fast removal in an emergency.

options.text: Two fingers fit under the cuff
options.rationale: Correct fit that protects circulation and skin.

options.text: The call light is placed in the client's hand
options.rationale: Correct. A restrained client must be able to call.

questions.takeaway: Restraint straps attach to the part of the bed frame that moves with the client, with a quick-release tie and two fingers of space.
questions.strategy: You are hunting the unsafe one. Picture the side rail being lowered with the strap attached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the error.
Quick release, two fingers, call light.
The arm goes with it.

elimination.verdict: The strap tied to the side rail.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report that a client on fall precautions seems much more unsteady walking than this morning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to turn on the bed alarm
options.rationale: A safe step and tempting. It adds a measure before anyone knows why she changed.

options.text: Go assess the client's gait and condition
options.rationale: A change in status needs the nurse's assessment before the plan is changed.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to recheck her gait in an hour
options.rationale: Evaluating a change cannot be delegated, and waiting leaves a new problem unexamined.

options.text: Request a physical therapy consult
options.rationale: May follow. The nurse has to know what changed first.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel report concerning behavior. Assessing fall risk, setting the plan and evaluating it stay with the nurse.
questions.strategy: The report is a cue, not an assessment. Pick the option where the nurse gathers the data.

steps.detail: Only a secondhand report.
Rechecking gait is assessment.
Alarm and consult wait for findings.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client now.

questions.stem: A client in bed begins a tonic-clonic seizure, lying supine with gurgling secretions. The teeth are clenched. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Suction the mouth with an oral catheter
options.rationale: Aims at the airway, so it tempts. Nothing is forced between clenched teeth.

options.text: Note the time and page the provider
options.rationale: Timing matters and takes a glance. Leaving the airway to make a call does not protect him.

options.text: Turn the client onto his side
options.rationale: Lets secretions drain and keeps the airway clear without entering the mouth.

options.text: Pad the side rails with blankets
options.rationale: Protects from injury after the airway is secured.

questions.takeaway: In a seizure, airway comes first and it is protected by positioning. Nothing goes in the mouth.
questions.strategy: Two options address the airway. The clenched teeth rule one of them out.

steps.detail: Suction and side lying.
Suction through the mouth is out.
Timing and padding follow.

elimination.verdict: Turn him onto his side.

questions.stem: A client at high fall risk was taught to call before getting up. Which finding indicates the teaching was effective?

options.text: He says he understands why he should call
options.rationale: Stated understanding is not behavior.

options.text: He correctly repeats the steps for using the call light
options.rationale: Better, and tempting. It still shows knowledge and not use.

options.text: His wife says she will remind him to call
options.rationale: Family support helps. It does not show what he does.

options.text: He presses the call light and waits before standing
options.rationale: He used the device and waited, which is the outcome the teaching aimed for.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate safety teaching by what the client does. Have the client demonstrate call light use.
questions.strategy: Line the options up from saying to doing. The strongest evidence is the behavior itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calls and waits.
Understanding and repeating steps.
The wife's reminder.

elimination.verdict: He presses the light and waits.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a client who is weak, at high fall risk and able to follow directions. Which tasks can the nurse assign to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walk the client to the bathroom with a gait belt per the plan
options.rationale: Assisting with mobility according to the plan can be delegated.

options.text: Decide whether the client is ready to walk without the belt
options.rationale: Judging readiness is evaluation, which stays with the nurse.

options.text: Keep the floor dry and the path to the bathroom clear
options.rationale: Maintaining a safe environment can be delegated.

options.text: Offer toileting on the schedule the nurse set
options.rationale: Assisting with toileting on a set schedule can be delegated.

options.text: Report if the client tries to get up without calling
options.rationale: Reporting concerning behavior is expected of assistive personnel.

options.text: Complete the fall risk score after the new sedative is started
options.rationale: Fall risk assessment is the nurse's responsibility, especially after a change.

questions.takeaway: The nurse assesses, plans and evaluates. Assistive personnel assist with toileting and mobility, keep the environment safe and report.
questions.strategy: Test each option for a judgment word such as decide or score. Doing and reporting can go; judging cannot.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Deciding readiness and scoring risk.
Walking, toileting and clearing the floor.
Telling the nurse about unsafe attempts.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A client is found on the floor, alert, reporting severe hip pain. One leg is shorter and turned outward. A coworker offers to help lift him to bed. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Lift him to bed with the coworker, then assess
options.rationale: Comfortable and tempting. Moving a likely fracture before assessment can worsen the injury.

options.text: Keep him still on the floor and complete the injury assessment
options.rationale: The leg findings suggest a fracture, so he is not moved until he is assessed and can be moved safely.

options.text: Help him to a chair and take vital signs
options.rationale: Sitting him up puts weight and motion through the injured hip.

options.text: Leave the coworker with him and call the provider
options.rationale: Notification comes after the nurse has assessment findings to report.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, stay and assess for injury before moving the client. Signs of fracture mean he stays where he is.
questions.strategy: The shortened, rotated leg is the detail that decides it. Any option that moves him first is out.

steps.detail: Shorter and turned outward suggests a hip fracture.
Bed and chair both move the hip.
Assess, then notify.

elimination.verdict: Keep him still and assess.

questions.stem: After a client fell at night walking to the bathroom, the nurse added toileting rounds every two hours. Which finding three nights later indicates the change is effective?

options.text: No falls, and an indwelling catheter is now in place
options.rationale: No fall, and tempting. The catheter removed the need and adds infection risk. It does not show the rounds worked.

options.text: No falls, and all four side rails are raised at night
options.rationale: Rails that confine him are a restraint and raise the risk of injury from climbing.

options.text: No falls, and he voids with staff on each round
options.rationale: The urgency is met on schedule and he no longer gets up alone.

options.text: No falls, and he limits fluids after dinner
options.rationale: He is avoiding the need on his own, which risks dehydration.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate a targeted intervention by whether it met the need that caused the fall, without adding a new harm.
questions.strategy: Every option says no falls. Look at the second half for how the result was reached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No falls appears four times.
Catheter, four rails, fluid restriction.
Voiding with staff on rounds.

elimination.verdict: Voids with staff on each round.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old insists on walking to the bathroom alone at night as she does at home. She is steady by day but has new nighttime dizziness. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Agree with her on a night light and assistance for night trips only
options.rationale: Keeps her daytime routine, targets the new limitation and makes her part of the plan.

options.text: Require staff assistance for all walking, day and night
options.rationale: Safe and tempting. It restricts abilities she still has and ignores her routine.

options.text: Turn on a bed alarm without discussing it with her
options.rationale: Decides for her and does not use what she can tell you about her habits.

options.text: Document her refusal and let her walk alone
options.rationale: Respects her choice and leaves the new dizziness unaddressed.

questions.takeaway: See safety through the client's eyes: learn the home routine, separate normal abilities from new limitations and plan with the client.
questions.strategy: Find the option that matches the restriction to what is new and involves her in the decision.

steps.detail: Steady by day, dizzy at night.
Help with everything, or no plan.
She agrees to night help and a light.

elimination.verdict: Night light and night assistance, agreed with her.

questions.stem: A client in wrist restraints for pulling at his tracheostomy has been quiet for an hour. He no longer pulls at the tube and does not open his eyes to his name. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Release one wrist as a trial of removal
options.rationale: Tempting because calm behavior is the cue to remove restraints early. This quiet is not calm; he is not responding, so the cause comes first.

options.text: Check his breathing and level of consciousness
options.rationale: He does not rouse to his name. Quiet with a drop in responsiveness is a change in mental status, and with a tracheostomy the airway is checked first.

options.text: Continue the restraints and recheck on schedule
options.rationale: Tempting because the pulling stopped. Waiting leaves an unresponsive client unassessed.

options.text: Ask the provider to discontinue the order
options.rationale: The right goal once he is calm and safe. It skips the finding that he will not open his eyes.

questions.takeaway: A restrained client who goes quiet is not automatically better. Mental status is part of every restraint check.
questions.strategy: Ask what changed: the behavior stopped, and so did his response to his name. One is good news and one is not.

steps.detail: He no longer pulls, and he does not rouse.

steps.action: Cut the options that assume improvement
steps.detail: Trial release and discontinuing both treat this as calm.
A scheduled recheck leaves a new change unassessed.

elimination.verdict: Assess breathing and responsiveness first.

questions.stem: After report, the nurse has four clients. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: In a vest restraint, shouting that he needs the toilet
options.rationale: A real unmet need that should be answered soon, and the likely cause of his agitation. He is alert and voicing it, so he is not deteriorating.

options.text: Had a seizure ten minutes ago, sleepy and slow to answer
options.rationale: Looks alarming, and drowsiness after a seizure is expected. He is breathing and rousable.

options.text: Fell an hour ago uninjured, now repeats the same question
options.rationale: New repetitive questioning after a fall is a change in mental status and suggests a head injury that the first check missed. It is the only unexpected finding.

options.text: Confused, sitting at the bed edge with assistive personnel beside her
options.rationale: A fall waiting to happen, which makes it tempting. Staff are at her side, so the risk is controlled for now.

questions.takeaway: After a fall, a new change in thinking outranks louder problems. Unexpected beats expected.
questions.strategy: All four need you. Ask which finding is new and not explained by what you already know about the client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sleepiness after a seizure is the postictal state.
The confused client has staff beside her.
A toileting need is voiced by an alert client. Repeating questions after a fall is a new brain cue.

elimination.verdict: The client who fell and is now repeating himself.

questions.stem: A client with delirium has pulled out two IV lines despite reorientation, a covered site and a sitter at the bedside. He is now gripping his chest tube. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Apply mitts and obtain a restraint order
options.rationale: Alternatives were tried and failed, and pulling a chest tube is immediate serious harm. Mitts are the least restrictive device that stops the grip.

options.text: Have the sitter reorient him more often
options.rationale: Least restrictive, which is usually the right rule. The stem shows it already failed twice and the harm is now immediate.

options.text: Request a sedative to calm him
options.rationale: Tempting as a quick fix. A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint and is more restrictive than mitts.

options.text: Move him to a room near the station
options.rationale: A reasonable alternative for observation. He already has a sitter within reach and still pulled lines.

questions.takeaway: Least restrictive means the least that works. When alternatives have failed and harm is immediate, a restraint is indicated.
questions.strategy: Two rules compete: least restrictive and prevent immediate harm. Check whether the stem says alternatives were already tried.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reorientation, covering the site and a sitter all failed.
A pulled chest tube is serious and immediate.

steps.action: Pick the least restrictive thing that works
steps.detail: Mitts restrict less than wrist ties or a sedative.

elimination.verdict: Mitts with an order.

questions.stem: After a client's night fall, a bed alarm and two-hour toileting rounds were added. Three nights later he has not fallen, and the alarm sounds five times nightly as he gets up to urinate. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The plan is effective and should continue
options.rationale: No falls looks like success. The alarm is catching him each time, so the cause of the falls is still there.

options.text: The toileting schedule is not meeting his urgency
options.rationale: He still gets up alone five times a night. The rounds are not matched to when he needs to go, so the risk is unchanged.

options.text: He needs a sitter at night to stay safe
options.rationale: A defensible safety step. It watches the behavior without fixing the urgency that drives it.

options.text: The alarm should be changed to a quieter setting
options.rationale: Sleep disruption is a real concern. It does nothing about the unsafe attempts.

questions.takeaway: No falls is not the same as no risk. Evaluate whether the intervention removed the cause.
questions.strategy: Look past the outcome to the behavior. If the alarm is doing all the work, the targeted intervention is failing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Zero falls in three nights.
Five unassisted attempts each night to urinate.
Urgency was the target, and urgency is still getting him up.

elimination.verdict: The toileting schedule needs revising.

questions.stem: A tonic-clonic seizure has just ended. The client lies on his side, drowsy and confused, with noisy snoring breaths and an oxygen saturation of 96%. His wife asks the nurse to wake him. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Suction his mouth and throat right away
options.rationale: Noisy breathing points to the airway, so this tempts. He is side-lying with a saturation of 96%, so the airway is open and draining.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and offer water
options.rationale: Comforting to the family. A drowsy client can aspirate.

options.text: Rouse him fully to check his orientation
options.rationale: Assessment sounds right. Confusion and sleep are expected now, and the airway data are already in hand.

options.text: Keep him side-lying and stay while he rests
options.rationale: Drowsiness and confusion are expected after a seizure. Side-lying protects the airway, and 96% shows it is working.

questions.takeaway: After a seizure, sleepiness is expected. Protect the airway by position, stay, and let the client recover.
questions.strategy: Airway comes first, so ask whether the airway is actually threatened. The saturation answers that.

steps.detail: Noisy breaths, side-lying, saturation 96%.
Drowsy and confused is the postictal state.
Water and sitting up are unsafe for a drowsy client.

elimination.verdict: Side-lying, stay with him, let him rest.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old one day after surgery sits unsupported at the bedside and shakes the nurse's hand across midline. She cannot straighten either knee. Which plan does the nurse choose for moving her to the chair?

options.text: Stand her with a gait belt and a walker
options.rationale: Tempting because she sits so well. Legs that cannot extend at the knee will not hold her in standing.

options.text: Use a mechanical lift for the transfer
options.rationale: She passed sitting balance and failed leg strength, so she cannot help stand. Equipment does the lifting.

options.text: Have two assistive personnel pivot her to the chair
options.rationale: More hands still means lifting her weight, which injures staff and can drop her.

options.text: Keep her in bed until her legs are stronger
options.rationale: Safe today, and it adds another day of the immobility that is weakening her.

questions.takeaway: Each bedside mobility test she fails sets the equipment. Good sitting balance with no leg strength means a lift, not a walker and not bed rest.
questions.strategy: Two options feel safe: the lift and staying in bed. The stem says she can sit, so she can be up in a chair; it also says her knees will not extend, so she cannot stand.

steps.detail: Knees will not straighten, so standing options are out.
Two people lifting is not safe handling.
She can sit, so the chair is still the goal.

elimination.verdict: Mechanical lift. Out of bed, without asking her legs to do what they cannot.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old on bed rest for 5 days walks in the hall for the first time. Which findings mean the nurse stops the walk and sits him down? Select all that apply.

options.text: He says the hallway is starting to spin
options.rationale: Dizziness during activity signals poor brain perfusion and a fall about to happen.

options.text: His face is pale and wet with sweat
options.rationale: Diaphoresis and pallor show the heart is not keeping up with the demand.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 94
options.rationale: A modest rise is the expected response to walking.

options.text: He reports new pressure in his chest
options.rationale: Chest pain with exertion means the heart muscle is short of oxygen. Stop the demand.

options.text: Respirations rise from 16 to 20 with easy speech
options.rationale: A small rise with comfortable talking is normal exertion, not dyspnea.

options.text: He says his legs feel a little tired
options.rationale: Mild fatigue after 5 days in bed is expected. Shorten the distance, but it is not a stop sign.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by the response. Dizziness, diaphoresis, chest pain and dyspnea end the walk. A modest rise in rate that recovers does not.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into the body working harder, which is expected, or the body failing to keep up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Small rises in heart rate and breathing with easy speech, plus mild leg fatigue.
Spinning, pale and sweaty, chest pressure.

elimination.verdict: Dizziness, diaphoresis and chest pressure stop the walk.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with left leg weakness is taught to walk with a straight cane. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Cane in the right hand, moved forward before the left leg
options.rationale: The cane goes on the strong side and leads, so it shares the load when the weak leg steps.

options.text: Cane in the left hand, moved forward with the left leg
options.rationale: Feels natural to put support beside the weak leg, but it shifts weight toward that side and narrows the base.

options.text: Cane in the right hand, moved forward after the right leg
options.rationale: Right side is correct, but stepping strong leg first leaves the weak leg bearing weight alone.

options.text: Cane in the left hand, kept a full stride ahead
options.rationale: Wrong side, and a long reach pulls him off balance.

questions.takeaway: Cane on the stronger side. Cane, then weak leg, then strong leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
questions.strategy: Two things have to be right: which hand and which order. Check the hand against the stem first, then the order.

steps.detail: Weak leg is the left, so the cane is in the right hand. Two options drop out.
The cane must be down before the weak leg takes weight.

elimination.verdict: Right hand, cane first, then the left leg.

questions.stem: A nurse walks a patient with a gait belt. Ten feet from the nearest chair his knees buckle and he starts to go down. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold him upright by the belt and call for help
options.rationale: A gait belt steadies; it is not for holding a collapsing adult's weight.

options.text: Support him under the arm and hurry to the chair
options.rationale: Tempting because a chair is the planned rescue. His knees have already buckled, so he cannot take those steps.

options.text: Widen her stance and ease him down her leg to the floor
options.rationale: A controlled descent protects his head and her back when the fall has already started.

options.text: Let go and move the furniture out of his path
options.rationale: Clearing hazards matters, but releasing him turns a guided descent into a free fall.

questions.takeaway: Once a patient is going down, you do not stop the fall. You guide it: wide base, slide him down your leg, protect the head.
questions.strategy: The chair option is right for a patient who feels faint and can still step. Buckled knees ten feet away tip it to the floor.

steps.detail: He is already falling, not just dizzy.
That is a lift by the belt.
Ten feet with no leg strength is not reachable.

elimination.verdict: Guide him to the floor.

questions.stem: Two hours after a forearm cast is applied, the patient's fingers are cool and pale with new tingling, and pain is rising despite an analgesic. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck color and capillary refill in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Reassessment is usually right, but these findings are already abnormal and tissue is at risk while you wait.

options.text: Give the next analgesic dose when it is due
options.rationale: Pain that climbs despite medication is the warning sign, not the problem to treat.

options.text: Cover the hand with a warm blanket
options.rationale: Treats the cool skin and leaves the cause, pressure inside the cast, untouched.

options.text: Notify the provider now
options.rationale: Cool, pale, tingling and worsening pain are red flags for lost circulation. The assessment is done and the fix needs a provider.

questions.takeaway: Sudden change in color, temperature, sensation or pain in a limb is reported at once. Do not keep collecting data you already have.
questions.strategy: Assess first is the reflex, but the stem hands you a complete neurovascular check with three abnormal results. The next step is action.

steps.detail: Nothing. Color, temperature, sensation and pain are all given.
Blanket and analgesic treat symptoms.
Waiting 30 minutes costs tissue.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: A patient with right-sided weakness after a stroke can lift her right arm halfway to shoulder height but no farther. Which exercise plan fits her right shoulder?

options.text: She lifts as far as she can, then the nurse completes the range
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion uses the muscle she has and still takes the joint through its full range.

options.text: The nurse moves the arm through the full range while she relaxes
options.rationale: Protects the joint, and tempting because the arm is weak. It wastes the strength she has, so the muscle keeps shrinking.

options.text: She lifts the arm halfway ten times each hour on her own
options.rationale: Keeps the muscle working, but the top half of the range is never reached and will stiffen.

options.text: She presses the arm against the mattress and holds
options.rationale: Isometric work builds static strength without moving the joint, so range is not maintained.

questions.takeaway: Match range of motion to what the patient can do: active if she can do it all, active-assistive if partway, passive only if not at all.
questions.strategy: Passive and active-assistive both protect the joint. Halfway on her own is the detail that says use her muscle.

steps.detail: Half the range, actively.

steps.action: Cut options that skip full range
steps.detail: Halfway only, and isometric holds.
Only one keeps both the muscle and the joint.

elimination.verdict: She moves it, the nurse finishes it.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for a week has sequential compression devices on and does ankle pumps hourly. Which finding shows these measures are working?

options.text: Pedal pulses strong and equal in both feet
options.rationale: Good to find, and tempting because it sounds like circulation. Pulses are arterial; these measures target venous return.

options.text: Blood pressure steady while lying flat
options.rationale: Supine pressure says nothing about venous stasis or clot.

options.text: Calves equal in size, soft and nontender
options.rationale: The goal is no thrombus from venous stasis. Equal, soft, painless calves are the evidence.

options.text: The sleeves are on whenever the nurse checks
options.rationale: That shows the intervention was done, not that it worked.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate against the goal. Leg exercises and compression aim at venous stasis, so you look at the calves.
questions.strategy: Ask what each finding measures. One measures arteries, one measures compliance, one measures the veins the plan is protecting.

steps.detail: Prevent venous stasis and thrombus.
Sleeves on is process, not outcome.
Pulses are arterial flow.

elimination.verdict: Equal, soft, nontender calves.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients who have been on bed rest for a week. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: One who was dizzy on sitting up and feels fine lying down
options.rationale: Orthostatic and expected after a week in bed. Symptoms resolved with position.

options.text: One with sudden shortness of breath and chest pain after standing
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea and chest pain after immobility suggest a clot has moved to the lung. Breathing comes first.

options.text: One with a red heel that blanches when pressed
options.rationale: Blanching redness is early and reversible. Offload it soon.

options.text: One with no bowel movement in 3 days
options.rationale: Uncomfortable and expected with slowed motility. Not urgent.

questions.takeaway: All four are effects of immobility. The one that is sudden and touches breathing is seen first.
questions.strategy: Sort expected from unexpected, then apply airway, breathing, circulation to what is left.

steps.detail: Constipation, blanching redness, resolved dizziness.
Sudden dyspnea with chest pain is new and unstable.

elimination.verdict: The patient with sudden shortness of breath.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old woman is admitted for a urinary tract infection. The nurse completes a musculoskeletal assessment and compares both sides.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with aging or requires follow-up.

rows.text: Lost 1.5 inches of height over 10 years
rows.rationale: Gradual bone loss and disk thinning shorten the spine slowly.

rows.text: Walks more slowly than she did at 60
rows.rationale: Movement slows as muscle mass declines.

rows.text: Right knee swollen and warm since yesterday
rows.rationale: One-sided, new and inflamed. Aging is gradual and symmetric.

rows.text: Both shoulders reach slightly less overhead
rows.rationale: Cartilage is less elastic, so range drops on both sides equally.

rows.text: Left foot has dragged for the past 3 days
rows.rationale: New one-sided loss of movement points to nerve injury or stroke.

rows.text: Thighs slightly thinner on both sides
rows.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Symmetry is the reassuring detail.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual and equal on both sides. Sudden or one-sided findings are not aging.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each row: did it come on slowly, and is it the same on both sides? Two yes answers mean aging.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Yesterday and 3 days are sudden. Ten years is gradual.
Right knee and left foot are one-sided.

elimination.verdict: The swollen knee and the dragging foot need follow-up. The rest is aging.

questions.stem: A patient straightens each knee at the bedside, then lifts his buttocks off the bed but drops back after 2 seconds. He needs the bathroom. Which plan does the nurse choose?

options.text: Walk him with a walker and standby assist
options.rationale: A walker helps balance. It does not supply the leg strength he just showed he lacks.

options.text: Walk him with a gait belt and one staff member
options.rationale: A gait belt steadies a patient who can stand; it cannot hold him up.

options.text: Offer a urinal in bed until he can stand longer
options.rationale: Safe, and tempting after a failed stand. It skips the weight bearing he can do and adds immobility.

options.text: Use a sit-to-stand lift to take him to the toilet
options.rationale: He has some leg strength but cannot hold a stand for a count of 5. The lift lets him bear weight safely.

questions.takeaway: A patient who can start a stand but not hold it is moderate assist. Use equipment that lets him use his legs without relying on them.
questions.strategy: The urinal and the lift are both safe. He has usable leg strength, so pick the safe option that keeps him moving.

steps.detail: He could not hold the hover for 5, so walking is out.
Both prevent a fall. Only one preserves function.

elimination.verdict: Sit-to-stand lift.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old who cannot bear weight on the left foot is taught to use axillary crutches. Which observation shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Crutch pads sit snug in the axillae as he swings through
options.rationale: Feels stable, and it puts body weight on the axillary nerves.

options.text: Weight rests on his hands with a gap below each axilla
options.rationale: Hands carry the weight. Space under the arm keeps pressure off the nerves in the axilla.

options.text: Elbows stay locked straight while he bears down
options.rationale: A slight bend lets the arms absorb load. Locked elbows mean the crutches are too short or the grips too low.

options.text: Crutch tips land directly beside his toes
options.rationale: Tips belong ahead and to the side to form a wide tripod base.

questions.takeaway: With axillary crutches the hands bear the weight, never the armpits.
questions.strategy: The snug option sounds secure. Ask where his weight is going in each picture.

steps.detail: Snug in the axilla versus a gap below it.
Axilla pressure injures nerves. Hands are built for it.

elimination.verdict: Weight on the hands with a gap under the arms.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old who takes insulin for diabetes plans to start brisk 40-minute walks after work. Which instruction does the nurse include?

options.text: Check glucose before walking and carry a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: Exercise pulls glucose into muscle on top of the insulin. Checking and carrying sugar manages the low.

options.text: Skip the insulin dose on days he walks
options.rationale: Removes the low and risks high glucose. The dose is adjusted by the provider, not dropped.

options.text: Keep walks under 10 minutes to protect his glucose
options.rationale: Avoids the risk by giving up the benefit. The plan is modified, not cancelled.

options.text: Walk right after the insulin dose for best effect
options.rationale: Exercising as insulin acts makes hypoglycemia more likely.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness changes the exercise plan; it does not remove it. For insulin users the change is glucose checks and a carbohydrate on hand.
questions.strategy: Three options avoid the low by breaking something else. One lets him keep both the insulin and the walk.

steps.detail: Low glucose during or after the walk.

steps.action: Cut the options that sacrifice treatment or exercise
steps.detail: Skipped insulin, 10-minute cap.
Walking as insulin acts raises the risk.

elimination.verdict: Check first and carry sugar.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic neuropathy has full leg strength. He stands steady with eyes open and sways badly with eyes closed. The findings are most consistent with which problem?

options.text: Weakness of the leg muscles
options.rationale: Strength was tested and is full.

options.text: A drop in blood pressure on standing
options.rationale: That would cause dizziness with eyes open as well.

options.text: Stiffness of the ankle joints
options.rationale: Stiff joints limit range. They do not change with eye closure.

options.text: Loss of position sense in the feet
options.rationale: Steady with vision and unsteady without it means his eyes were covering for missing proprioception.

questions.takeaway: Balance needs muscle, joint and nerve input. When closing the eyes unmasks sway, the missing piece is proprioception, so the plan is lighting and visual cues.
questions.strategy: Find the detail that changes: only the eyes. Pick the cause that vision could compensate for.

steps.detail: Full strength rules out weakness.
Blood pressure and stiff ankles would not care whether he can see.

elimination.verdict: Loss of position sense.

questions.stem: A patient with coronary artery disease is walking the hall with the nurse and reports pressure in his chest. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Measure his blood pressure and pulse
options.rationale: Needed, and tempting as assess first. He has already given the key cue, and standing while you measure keeps the demand up.

options.text: Walk him slowly back to his room
options.rationale: More walking is more demand.

options.text: Stop the walk and sit him in the nearest chair
options.rationale: Chest pressure on exertion means demand exceeds supply. Rest lowers demand in seconds.

options.text: Ask him to rate the pressure from 0 to 10
options.rationale: Useful once he is seated. It delays the one thing that helps.

questions.takeaway: When activity causes the symptom, stopping the activity is the first action. Vital signs come with him sitting.
questions.strategy: Assessment usually leads. Here the symptom is the assessment, and the cause is still happening until he sits.

steps.detail: Exertion.
Walking back to the room.
Sit first, then vital signs and a pain rating.

elimination.verdict: Stop and sit him down.

questions.stem: An unresponsive patient receives passive range of motion to both elbows three times a day. Which finding after 2 weeks shows the exercise is effective?

options.text: Upper arm muscles look fuller than before
options.rationale: Tempting as a sign of progress. Passive motion does not contract muscle, so it cannot build bulk.

options.text: Both elbows extend fully without resistance
options.rationale: Passive motion exists to keep joints mobile and prevent contracture. Full, easy range is the goal met.

options.text: Skin over both elbows is intact
options.rationale: Reflects turning and pressure relief, not joint exercise.

options.text: He withdraws his arms when they are moved
options.rationale: A change in responsiveness, and possibly a sign of pain. It does not measure joint mobility.

questions.takeaway: Passive range of motion maintains joints. It does not build strength. Evaluate it by range, not by muscle.
questions.strategy: Ask what the intervention can do. A nurse moving the arm cannot make the muscle grow.

steps.detail: Flexible joints, no contracture.

steps.action: Cut what belongs to other interventions
steps.detail: Skin and responsiveness.
Only range is in passive motion's reach.

elimination.verdict: Full extension without resistance.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD began a walking program last week. Which finding today shows activity tolerance has improved?

options.text: Walks 250 feet, stopping twice for breath, saturation 86%
options.rationale: Farther is tempting. Dyspnea and desaturation show he exceeded his tolerance, not improved it.

options.text: Says he feels more motivated to walk
options.rationale: Worth supporting. Motivation is not a physiologic response.

options.text: Resting heart rate is the same as last week
options.rationale: Resting values do not show how he responds to activity.

options.text: Walks 150 feet and heart rate recovers in 3 minutes, down from 10
options.rationale: Same work with faster recovery and no distress is what better tolerance looks like.

questions.takeaway: Tolerance is measured by the response to activity and the recovery after it, not by distance alone.
questions.strategy: Distance draws the eye. Read what came with the distance.

steps.detail: Motivation and resting rate.
One recovers quickly. One ends in low saturation.

elimination.verdict: Faster recovery at the same distance.

questions.stem: During passive range of motion, the nurse feels the patient's shoulder resist at 90 degrees of abduction and the patient grimaces. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Stop at that point and return the arm to rest
options.rationale: Resistance and pain mark the limit. Forcing past it tears tissue.

options.text: Hold a gentle stretch just past the resistance
options.rationale: Sounds like therapy and is how joints get injured in a patient who cannot protect them.

options.text: Skip the shoulder for the rest of the week
options.rationale: Avoids pain and lets the joint stiffen further. Exercise continues within the limit.

options.text: Move the arm faster to get through the tight spot
options.rationale: Speed adds force and removes the nurse's ability to feel the limit.

questions.takeaway: Range of motion goes to the point of resistance or pain and no farther. Note the limit and compare with the other side.
questions.strategy: Two options give up range and two push for it. The stem gives two stop signals at once.

steps.detail: Resistance plus a grimace.
Stretching past it or speeding through.

steps.action: Compare stopping now with stopping for a week
steps.detail: Only one keeps the joint moving.

elimination.verdict: Stop at the resistance.

questions.stem: A patient immobile after a stroke has a weak cough with coarse crackles, a heel that stays red when pressed and no bowel movement in 4 days. Which problem does the nurse address first?

options.text: The nonblanching heel
options.rationale: An actual injury and the strong runner-up. It is offloaded next, but it does not threaten oxygenation.

options.text: Constipation
options.rationale: Real and uncomfortable. It can wait behind lungs and skin.

options.text: Retained secretions
options.rationale: Secretions he cannot clear lead to atelectasis and pneumonia. Breathing outranks skin.

options.text: Risk for contracture
options.rationale: A potential problem, behind the actual ones.

questions.takeaway: When several immobility effects are present at once, rank them by airway and breathing first, then actual tissue injury, then the rest.
questions.strategy: The heel and the lungs are both actual problems. Breathing breaks the tie.

steps.detail: Contracture has not happened.
Constipation.
Lungs before skin.

elimination.verdict: Retained secretions.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old on bed rest for 4 days takes a new antihypertensive and will walk for the first time. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed, then sit her at the bedside to dangle
options.rationale: Second. A staged position change lets her circulation adjust.

options.text: Apply a gait belt and stand her at the bedside
options.rationale: Fourth. She stands only after sitting is tolerated, with the belt on.

options.text: Check her baseline blood pressure and pulse lying down
options.rationale: First. You need a baseline to judge what happens when she sits.

options.text: Walk a short distance with a chair close by
options.rationale: Last. Distance comes after she has passed sitting and standing.

options.text: Ask about dizziness and recheck blood pressure while she sits
options.rationale: Third. This is the checkpoint that decides whether she goes on.

questions.takeaway: First time up after bed rest is staged: baseline, sit and dangle, reassess, stand, then walk.
questions.strategy: Bed rest plus an antihypertensive means the pressure will drop. Put a check before and after the first position change.

steps.detail: Lying vital signs come before any movement.
Sit, then stand, then walk.
Symptoms and pressure are rechecked while sitting, before standing.

elimination.verdict: Baseline, dangle, reassess, stand with belt, walk.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman whose bone density scan shows low bone mass is taught about exercise. Which statement shows she understood?

options.text: "I will swim laps every morning for my bones."
options.rationale: Good exercise and the tempting choice. Water carries her weight, so the bones are not loaded.

options.text: "I will walk briskly for 30 minutes most days."
options.rationale: Walking loads the skeleton. Bone responds to weight bearing.

options.text: "I will rest more so I do not break anything."
options.rationale: Inactivity speeds bone loss.

options.text: "I will ride my stationary bike in place of walking."
options.rationale: Good for the heart. The seat carries her weight, so it does less for bone than walking.

questions.takeaway: Bone is kept by loading it. For low bone mass the exercise has to be weight bearing.
questions.strategy: Three options are exercise. Ask which one has her bones carrying her weight.

steps.detail: Immobility demineralizes bone.
Water and a bike seat carry the weight for her.

elimination.verdict: Brisk walking most days.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients on bed rest for six days. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: One calf is warm, swollen and tender to touch
options.rationale: A likely clot and an actual problem, so it is a strong runner up. It is still in the leg; another client shows where a clot goes next.

options.text: Dizzy on sitting up, now lying flat and comfortable
options.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is expected after bed rest and resolved when he lay down.

options.text: One heel stays red when pressed with a finger
options.rationale: Early pressure injury that needs offloading. It is not a threat in the next minutes.

options.text: Sore calf yesterday, now anxious and breathing fast
options.rationale: A sore calf followed by sudden anxiety and fast breathing suggests the clot has moved to the lung. Breathing outranks the rest.

questions.takeaway: In an immobile client, new anxiety and fast breathing after calf soreness is a breathing problem until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: Two clients have calf findings. Ask which one has moved from circulation in the leg to breathing.

steps.detail: Dizziness that cleared lying flat is expected.
A red heel is early and local.
One is swollen. The other was sore and now the client cannot breathe easily.

elimination.verdict: The anxious client breathing fast.

questions.stem: A client has a lower leg cast applied yesterday. The foot is warm with a strong pulse. Pain is now severe, worse than yesterday and not eased by the analgesic given an hour ago. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Give the next dose early and recheck soon
options.rationale: Pain after a fracture is expected, so treating it tempts. Pain that is rising and not responding is a red flag, not a dosing problem.

options.text: Document that circulation to the foot is intact
options.rationale: The pulse and warmth are reassuring and true. They do not explain severe, worsening pain.

options.text: Notify the provider of the pain now
options.rationale: Severe pain that worsens and does not respond to medication is a reportable red flag even while the pulse is present.

options.text: Recheck the pulse and warmth every hour
options.rationale: More assessment sounds safe. The deciding finding is already known, and waiting for a lost pulse is waiting too long.

questions.takeaway: Do not let a good pulse reassure you. Severe, worsening pain that the analgesic does not touch is reported at once.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into reassuring and worrying. The quiet one is the pain that does not respond.

steps.detail: Warm foot and strong pulse.
Pain is worse than yesterday and unrelieved.
The assessment is done. Report it.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now.

questions.stem: After five days of bed rest a client dangles for two minutes. Blood pressure goes from 124/76 to 118/72, pulse from 78 to 114, and he says he feels fine. What does the nurse do next?

options.text: Keep him seated and recheck before standing
options.rationale: The pulse rose 36 beats to hold the pressure up. He is compensating, so he is not ready to stand yet.

options.text: Stand him with the gait belt as planned
options.rationale: The pressure barely moved and he feels fine, so this tempts. The pulse shows the pressure is being held up with effort.

options.text: Return him to bed and cancel walking today
options.rationale: Safe, and too far. Keeping him in bed worsens the deconditioning that caused this.

options.text: Have him march in place beside the bed
options.rationale: The next step in a mobility check. It needs standing, which he has not yet shown he tolerates.

questions.takeaway: A stable blood pressure with a big jump in pulse is not tolerance. Give the body time before the next position change.
questions.strategy: Read both numbers. The pressure looks fine only because the heart is working hard to keep it there.

steps.detail: A 6 point drop is small.
A rise of 36 beats is compensation.
Standing now is too fast and cancelling is too restrictive.

elimination.verdict: Stay seated and recheck.

questions.stem: A client with COPD walks 100 feet. Pulse rises from 84 to 108 and respirations to 28. Five minutes after sitting, pulse is 104 and respirations 28. What is the plan for the next walk?

options.text: Repeat the same 100 feet without changes
options.rationale: Reasonable if he had recovered. He did not return toward baseline in five minutes, so this distance is too much as designed.

options.text: Shorten the distance and add rest stops
options.rationale: He failed to recover after five minutes of rest. Keep him moving at a level he can recover from.

options.text: Increase to 150 feet to build endurance
options.rationale: Progressive activity is the goal. Progress follows tolerance, and he did not tolerate this.

options.text: Hold walking until the provider reassesses him
options.rationale: Protective, and immobility will lower his endurance further. Poor recovery calls for a smaller dose, not none.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is judged by recovery. If pulse and breathing stay up after rest, reduce the workload and keep the client moving.
questions.strategy: A rise during activity is expected. Look at the numbers after rest to decide.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read the response during the walk
steps.detail: Pulse and breathing rise, which is expected.
Still 104 and 28 after five minutes.
Less distance with rests, not more and not none.

elimination.verdict: Shorter distance with rest stops.

questions.stem: The nurse has four tasks waiting. Which one can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Walk a client who walked twice yesterday with one assist
options.rationale: A stable client with an established plan. Assisting with mobility according to the plan is delegable.

options.text: Apply compression devices to a client whose calf is newly tender
options.rationale: Applying the devices is routinely delegated, which tempts. A newly tender calf needs the nurse's assessment first.

options.text: Sit up a client for the first time after bed rest
options.rationale: Looks like routine mobility. A first time up needs the nurse to assess tolerance.

options.text: Reposition a client who reports new numbness in one foot
options.rationale: Turning is delegable. New numbness is a red flag that the nurse assesses before anyone moves the limb.

questions.takeaway: Delegate the task when the client is stable and the plan is set. Anything new or first belongs to the nurse.
questions.strategy: Every task is one assistive personnel can do. Look for the word that makes the client unstable: new or first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Newly tender calf and new numbness.
First time up after bed rest.
He walked twice yesterday on the same plan.

elimination.verdict: The client who already walked with one assist.

questions.stem: An alert 78-year-old with 3 days of diarrhea became dizzy the last time she stood. She now asks to walk to the bathroom. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Measure lying and standing blood pressures
options.rationale: Tempting because it is an assessment, but she already showed you she gets dizzy on standing. Standing her for a reading repeats the risk.

options.text: Have her sit at the bedside before standing with help
options.rationale: She is about to get up now, and a slow position change with assistance prevents the fall.

options.text: Offer a glass of oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Right treatment for an alert patient who can swallow, but it does not make this trip to the bathroom safe.

options.text: Request a prescription for IV fluids
options.rationale: She is alert and can drink, and it does nothing for the next two minutes.

questions.takeaway: Low volume plus a position change equals a fall. Slow the change and stay with her before you treat the volume.
questions.strategy: The stem already gives the assessment: she is dizzy when she stands. The question is what keeps her safe right now.

steps.detail: Dizziness on standing is in the stem, so more assessment adds nothing.
She is getting up now, so the action must work now.
Fluids fix the cause later. The slow, assisted position change prevents the injury.

elimination.verdict: Sit her at the bedside first, then stand with help.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving potassium chloride 10 mEq per hour through a forearm IV. She reports burning, and the site is red and swollen. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Slow the infusion to 5 mEq per hour
options.rationale: Tempting because a slower rate eases vein irritation, but swelling means the fluid may be in the tissue.

options.text: Apply a warm compress above the site
options.rationale: Does not stop potassium from entering damaged tissue.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: Burning with redness and swelling means the site has failed. Potassium in the tissue causes severe damage.

options.text: Reassess the site in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The site has already been assessed and it is abnormal. Waiting lets more potassium in.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium irritates veins and destroys tissue. Pain alone may mean slow it; pain with redness and swelling means stop it.
questions.strategy: Slowing and stopping are both real responses to a burning potassium site. The swelling is the detail that decides.

steps.detail: Burning, redness and swelling. The assessment is done.
Slowing treats irritation. Swelling points to infiltration, so the fluid must stop.
A compress or a recheck leaves the infusion running.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer and a calcium of 12.6 mg/dL is receiving 0.9% sodium chloride and furosemide. Which finding requires follow up first?

options.text: No bowel movement for 2 days
options.rationale: Expected with high calcium because the gut slows. It needs a plan and it is not urgent.

options.text: Reports feeling tired and weak
options.rationale: Expected with high calcium, which slows nerves and muscles.

options.text: Urine output of 150 mL per hour
options.rationale: This is the therapy working. Saline and furosemide flush calcium out through the kidneys.

options.text: Left calf warmer and larger than the right
options.rationale: High calcium raises clot risk in the legs. A clot can travel, so this is reported now.

questions.takeaway: In hypercalcemia, compare the calves. Slow gut and fatigue are expected; a warm, larger calf may be a clot.
questions.strategy: Three options are either expected or the goal of treatment. Ask which one is a new complication.

steps.detail: Brisk urine output is what saline and furosemide are for.
Constipation and weakness fit the calcium level.
One sided warmth and swelling suggests a clot.

elimination.verdict: The calf. Report it and do not massage it.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old taking a thiazide has a sodium of 124 mEq/L, a weak thready pulse and dry mucous membranes. Which prescription does the nurse clarify with the provider?

options.text: Fluid restriction of 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restriction is for low sodium from too much water. Her pulse and mouth show she has lost volume, so this would make her worse.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride IV infusion
options.rationale: Fits. She lost sodium and water, and isotonic saline replaces both.

options.text: Seizure precautions
options.rationale: Fits. A sodium of 124 puts the brain at risk.

options.text: Hold hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: Fits. The diuretic is the likely cause of the sodium loss.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium has two opposite treatments. A thready pulse and dry mouth mean loss, so she needs saline, not restriction.
questions.strategy: Fluid restriction is a correct hyponatremia order for a different patient. The pulse and mucous membranes tell you which patient this is.

steps.detail: You are looking for the order that does not fit.
Thready pulse and dry mucosa mean low volume.
Saline fits low volume. Restriction fits excess water.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the fluid restriction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with 2 days of vomiting had a blood pressure of 92/58 and urine output of 15 mL per hour. After 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride, which finding best indicates the bolus was effective?

options.text: Weight is 1 kg higher than on admission
options.rationale: Tempting, since 1 kg is 1 L. It only shows the fluid went in, not that the organs are perfused.

options.text: Reports feeling less thirsty
options.rationale: Subjective, and it lags behind what the vessels are doing.

options.text: Urine output is 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: The kidneys are being perfused again. Output above 30 mL per hour shows the vessels are refilled.

options.text: Urine is dark amber
options.rationale: Still concentrated, which means the deficit is not corrected.

questions.takeaway: To judge fluid replacement, look at perfusion. Urine output is the fastest honest sign that vascular volume is back.
questions.strategy: Weight and urine output both look like good news. One shows fluid was given; the other shows it worked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the finding that shows failure
steps.detail: Dark amber urine is still concentrated.
Thirst is not a reliable measure.
Weight records what was infused. Output shows the kidneys are perfused.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 45 mL per hour.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L has been receiving IV magnesium sulfate for 2 hours. Which finding requires the nurse's follow up?

options.text: Patellar reflexes are 2+, down from 4+
options.rationale: This is the goal. Reflexes were hyperactive and are now normal.

options.text: Respirations are 16 per minute
options.rationale: Normal. Toxicity slows breathing below 12.

options.text: Reports feeling warm during the infusion
options.rationale: A common, harmless effect of IV magnesium.

options.text: Urine output is 20 mL per hour
options.rationale: The kidneys clear magnesium. With low output the drug builds up and toxicity follows.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium leaves through the kidneys. Normal reflexes and breathing are reassuring now, and low urine output warns of what is coming.
questions.strategy: The reflexes and breathing are the usual toxicity checks and both are fine. Look for the finding that predicts trouble.

steps.detail: Reflexes present and respirations 16. No toxicity yet.
Warmth is common with the infusion.
Output below 30 mL per hour means magnesium is not being cleared.

elimination.verdict: Urine output of 20 mL per hour.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old with heart failure ate a salty holiday dinner yesterday. Today his weight is up 2.3 kg. He is short of breath lying flat and has new crackles in both lung bases.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed
options.rationale: He is short of breath lying flat. Sitting him up eases breathing right away.

options.text: Give furosemide as prescribed
options.rationale: A loop diuretic removes the extra fluid before it becomes pulmonary edema.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids
options.rationale: He already has too much fluid.

options.text: Start 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and adds to the overload.

options.text: Fluid overload with early pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Sudden weight gain, orthopnea and new crackles after a sodium load.

options.text: Isotonic dehydration
options.rationale: Dehydration brings weight loss and clear lungs.

options.text: Hyponatremia from sodium loss
options.rationale: He took in extra sodium, and nothing in the scenario shows a loss.

options.text: Hypokalemia
options.rationale: May follow the diuretic later. It does not explain today's findings.

options.text: Lung sounds
options.rationale: Crackles clearing or spreading tells you which way the lungs are going.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: The best indicator of fluid status, measured at the same time on the same scale.

options.text: Chvostek sign
options.rationale: A calcium and magnesium check.

options.text: Skin turgor over the sternum
options.rationale: A dehydration check, and he has the opposite problem.

questions.takeaway: A sudden weight gain with new crackles is overload heading toward pulmonary edema. Sit him up, remove fluid, then track lungs and weight.
questions.strategy: Decide the direction first. Every wrong option belongs to a patient who is dry.
