options.rationale: Stable and symmetric. Continue monthly self examination.

questions.takeaway: All changing lesions are referred. A multicolored, irregular, changing mole goes first because melanoma spreads.
questions.strategy: Bleeding draws the eye. Rank by which lesion can spread fastest, not by which looks worst today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Unchanged in photos.
Scaly patches and a pearly bump progress slowly.
A changing multicolored mole.

elimination.verdict: The changing mole.

questions.stem: A client with a Braden score of 15 sits in a chair most of the day and can stand with one person assisting. Which plan is best?

options.text: Assist the client to stand and march in place every hour
options.rationale: A client who can stand relieves pressure by standing and stepping about 5 times each hour.

options.text: Return the client to bed after one hour in the chair
options.rationale: Tempting because it limits sitting time. The client can stand, so bed rest gives up mobility without need.

options.text: Place a ring shaped cushion under the buttocks
options.rationale: Ring cushions press on the surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow.

options.text: Reposition the client in the chair every 2 hours
options.rationale: Two hours is the bed schedule. Sitting loads a smaller area and needs hourly relief.

questions.takeaway: Chair clients who are able stand and march in place 5 steps every hour. Use the client's own mobility before limiting activity.
questions.strategy: Use the detail that the client can stand. The best plan relieves pressure and keeps the client moving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Can stand with one assist.
Bed rest relieves pressure and costs mobility.
It damages capillaries.

elimination.verdict: Stand and march every hour.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with dry, itchy skin and nightly scratching completes teaching. Which statement indicates the plan is understood?

options.text: "I will soak in a hot bath each night before bed."
options.rationale: Hot water and daily soaking dry the skin further.

options.text: "I will rub my legs dry and then put on lotion."
options.rationale: Lotion is right. Rubbing irritates the skin, so the client should pat dry.

options.text: "I will dab rubbing alcohol on the spots that itch."
options.rationale: Alcohol and astringents dry the skin.

options.text: "I will take a full bath every other day in lukewarm water."
options.rationale: Less frequent bathing in tepid water keeps the skin's oils and breaks the itch and scratch cycle.

questions.takeaway: For dry skin itch: full bath every other day in tepid water, pat dry, moisturize, keep nails short, use a humidifier.
questions.strategy: One statement mixes a right step with a wrong one. Read each statement to the end.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hot water, alcohol and rubbing all dry or irritate.
Lotion is correct. Rubbing is not.
Every other day and lukewarm.

elimination.verdict: Bath every other day in lukewarm water.

questions.stem: A daughter asks for a swab culture of her father's open stage 3 injury. The wound is smaller with no odor, redness or fever. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Request a culture order so that treatment can start early
options.rationale: Tempting as the cautious choice. With a shrinking wound and no signs, a positive swab would lead to unneeded antibiotics.

options.text: Explain that the wound is watched for clinical signs of infection
options.rationale: Open pressure injuries are always colonized, so a swab grows bacteria anyway. Infection is judged by the wound and the client.

options.text: Request an antimicrobial dressing as a precaution
options.rationale: Antimicrobial dressings are for infected wounds. This one is healing.

options.text: Tell her a culture is unnecessary because the wound is healing
options.rationale: Dismisses the concern and gives her nothing to watch for.

questions.takeaway: Wound cultures are not routine for pressure injuries. Watch for spreading redness, a change in drainage, a larger wound, fever or a high white count.
questions.strategy: The assessment in the stem is already complete and reassuring. The right response uses it and still answers the daughter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smaller, no odor, no redness, no fever.
A colonized wound grows bacteria without being infected.
Explain what is being watched.

elimination.verdict: Explain clinical monitoring.

questions.stem: A daughter will care for her mother's stage 3 sacral injury at home. Which statements by the daughter indicate the discharge teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will show you how I take off the old dressing, clean the wound and put on a new one before we leave."
options.rationale: A return demonstration before discharge confirms the caregiver can do the care.

options.text: "I will call if the drainage changes color, smells bad or the skin around it gets redder."
options.rationale: These are the changes that are reported.

options.text: "I will give the pain medicine about half an hour before I change the dressing."
options.rationale: Pain is treated before dressing changes and repositioning.

options.text: "I will rub the red skin near the wound to bring the blood back."
options.rationale: Massage damages the capillaries in reddened skin.

options.text: "I will offer high protein snacks between meals."
options.rationale: Protein is needed to build new tissue.

options.text: "I will keep the wound open to air so it dries out."
options.rationale: Wounds heal in a moist, covered environment. Drying slows healing.

questions.takeaway: Home wound care teaching is effective when the caregiver demonstrates the dressing change, knows what to report, treats pain first and pushes protein.
questions.strategy: Two statements sound caring and harm the wound. Rubbing red skin and drying the wound both slow healing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Return demonstration, reporting changes, pain control, protein.
It injures reddened skin.
A moist wound bed heals.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with pressure injuries. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: Stage 4 sacral injury with tunneling and moderate drainage, unchanged this week
options.rationale: Looks the worst, and it is unchanged. A stable chronic wound can wait.

options.text: Unstageable heel injury covered with dry, intact eschar
options.rationale: Dry, stable eschar on a heel is left alone and offloaded. Expected.

options.text: Stage 2 sacral injury, new foul tan drainage, temperature 101.4 F
options.rationale: The stage is not the cue. A new change in the color and odor of drainage with a fever suggests infection that may be reaching the blood.

options.text: Heel deep tissue injury that opened to a shallow ulcer overnight
options.rationale: Tempting because it is a real change. Deep tissue injuries often open as they evolve, and this client has no sign of infection.

questions.takeaway: Do not rank pressure injuries by stage. New foul drainage with a fever means infection and outranks a deeper wound that is stable.
questions.strategy: Do not rank by stage. Look for the client with a new change plus a whole body sign.

steps.detail: Unchanged stage 4 and dry intact eschar.
One wound opened as expected. One has new foul drainage and a fever.
Fever with a drainage change points to infection that can spread.

elimination.verdict: The stage 2 injury with foul drainage and a fever.

questions.stem: A client was turned off a reddened left hip 30 minutes ago. The skin is intact, and the redness does not blanch. The AP asks whether the left side can stay in the turning schedule. Which response is correct?

options.text: "No. Keep him off that hip, and I will report it."
options.rationale: Redness that does not blanch after 30 minutes off the area is a stage 1 pressure injury. It is offloaded and reported.

options.text: "Yes. The skin is intact, so keep the 2 hour schedule."
options.rationale: Tempting because the skin is unbroken. Intact skin that does not blanch is already damaged, and more pressure deepens it.

options.text: "Not yet. I will check the blanching again in 30 minutes."
options.rationale: Tempting as assessment first. The blanch test is already done and gave the answer.

options.text: "Yes, after you rub in barrier cream to bring blood back."
options.rationale: Reddened areas are never massaged. Barrier cream is for moisture and does not treat pressure.

questions.takeaway: Blanchable redness means perfusion is intact. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is stage 1, so it stays offloaded.
questions.strategy: Intact skin sounds reassuring. The deciding word is in the blanch test.

steps.detail: Does not blanch after 30 minutes off the area.
Rubbing a red area adds damage.

steps.action: Choose action over a repeat test
steps.detail: The assessment is complete.

elimination.verdict: Keep him off the hip and report it.

questions.stem: A stage 3 sacral injury is slightly smaller than two weeks ago. The wound bed, then beefy red and moist, is now pale and dry with no drainage or odor. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: The wound is healing well, so continue the plan
options.rationale: Tempting because the wound is smaller and clean. Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist, and this bed has lost both.

options.text: The wound is infected, so request a wound culture
options.rationale: There is no odor, drainage change or redness, and cultures are not routine for pressure injuries.

options.text: The wound is ready to be left open to the air
options.rationale: A dry bed is the problem here. Open wounds heal in a moist environment.

options.text: Healing has stalled, so the change needs to be reported
options.rationale: Granulation that turns from beefy red to pale and dry means poor healing despite the smaller size. The change is reported so the plan can be reviewed.

questions.takeaway: Size alone does not prove healing. Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist. A bed that turns pale and dry is reported.
questions.strategy: One finding looks better. Check the wound bed against what healthy granulation looks like before you accept it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Beefy red, moist, slightly spongy.
This bed has gone from beefy red and moist to pale and dry.
No odor, drainage or redness.

elimination.verdict: Healing has stalled. Report the change.

questions.stem: A client has two lesions. One is 7 mm, round and evenly tan, unchanged in photos for 10 years. The other is 3 mm and in 2 months has darkened and developed two colors. Which conclusion guides the referral?

options.text: The 7 mm lesion is the greater concern because of its size
options.rationale: Tempting because it passes the 6 mm mark, and it is still checked. Ten years without change makes it the lesser concern.

options.text: The 3 mm lesion is the greater concern because it is changing
options.rationale: Evolving outranks the other ABCDE features. A small lesion that darkens and gains colors is the one referred first.

options.text: Both can wait for the next yearly skin examination
options.rationale: Any ABCDE feature is checked now, and a changing lesion does not wait a year.

options.text: Neither needs referral until a border becomes irregular
options.rationale: Each ABCDE feature counts by itself. Waiting for a second feature delays care.

questions.takeaway: Any one ABCDE feature gets a lesion checked. When features compete, evolving outranks diameter.
questions.strategy: Both lesions meet one ABCDE feature. Decide which feature carries more weight.

steps.action: Match each lesion to a letter
steps.detail: 7 mm is diameter. Darkening with two colors is color and evolving.
A changing lesion is not watched for a year.
Change beats size.

elimination.verdict: The small changing lesion goes first.

questions.stem: A heel injury was covered with dry, intact eschar last week. Today the eschar edge is soft and lifting, and the skin around it is red and warm. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Leave the eschar alone and keep the heel floated
options.rationale: Tempting because that is the rule for stable heel eschar. Soft edges with redness and warmth mean it is no longer stable.

options.text: Apply a hydrogel to soften the rest of the eschar
options.rationale: Softening eschar is a debridement decision that belongs to the provider.

options.text: Trim the loose eschar edge with sterile scissors
options.rationale: Sharp debridement is outside the nurse's role here and could cause bleeding.

options.text: Report the change for evaluation and possible debridement
options.rationale: The eschar is unstable and there are signs of infection, so the leave it alone rule no longer applies.

questions.takeaway: Heel eschar is left intact only while it is dry, stable and free of infection. Softening, lifting, redness or warmth gets reported.
questions.strategy: The familiar rule has conditions. Check whether this heel still meets them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Dry, intact, no infection.
Soft, lifting, red and warm fail all three.
The nurse reports. The provider decides on debridement.

elimination.verdict: Report it. The eschar is no longer stable.

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on NovoLog with meals has a fingerstick glucose of 64 mg/dL at 1150. He is alert and swallowing safely. His lunch tray is due in 10 minutes. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Wait for the tray and have him eat right away
options.rationale: Tempting because food is close and he looks well. A glucose under 70 is treated now with fast-acting carbohydrate. A mixed meal absorbs too slowly.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: He is under 70, alert and able to swallow, so the low is treated before anything else.

options.text: Give the NovoLog when the tray is set down
options.rationale: Insulin is never given to a client who is hypoglycemic.

options.text: Repeat the fingerstick on the other hand
options.rationale: The value is already known. Repeating it delays treatment.

questions.takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is treated now with 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, even when a meal is minutes away.
questions.strategy: Two options feed him. The glucose is already under 70, so pick the one that acts now with fast-acting carbohydrate.

steps.detail: 64 is under 70. That is hypoglycemia.

steps.action: Cut the insulin and the repeat stick
steps.detail: Insulin worsens a low. A second stick only delays.
A tray in 10 minutes is slower than carbohydrate now.

elimination.verdict: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate.

questions.stem: A student's first fingerstick on a 76-year-old with cold hands gave too small a drop. After coaching, which action on the second attempt shows the coaching was effective?

options.text: Punctures the center pad of the fingertip
options.rationale: The pad is more painful. The side of the fingertip is the taught site.

options.text: Squeezes the fingertip firmly to form a drop
options.rationale: Squeezing is the error to avoid.

options.text: Punctures while the washed finger is still damp
options.rationale: Residual water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Lowers the hand, then punctures the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Letting the hand hang down improves flow. The side of the fingertip gives a good sample.

questions.takeaway: Poor flow from a cold hand: warm gently or lower the hand, use the side of a dry fingertip, avoid squeezing.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that improves blood flow without changing the sample.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pad, squeezing and a damp finger are each errors.

steps.action: Find the one that fixes flow
steps.detail: A lowered hand brings blood to the fingertip.

elimination.verdict: Lowers the hand and punctures the side of the fingertip.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old received Humulin R and Humulin N in one syringe at 0730. She missed her afternoon snack and is shaky and sweating at 1600. Which explanation guides the nurse's follow-up?

options.text: The Humulin N is still within its peak
options.rationale: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose. At 1600 she is 8.5 hours in, with no snack to cover it.

options.text: The Humulin R is reaching its peak
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is the mealtime insulin. Its peak was 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which ended at 1130.

options.text: The two insulins cancelled each other in the syringe
options.rationale: Mixing regular and NPH is a prescribed practice. It does not cancel either dose.

options.text: The morning dose has worn off entirely
options.rationale: A dose that has worn off would produce a high, not signs of a low.

questions.takeaway: Count the hours from the dose. Regular peaks at 2 to 4 hours. NPH peaks at 4 to 12 hours, so an afternoon low after a morning mix belongs to the NPH.
questions.strategy: Do the clock math for each insulin before you choose. 0730 to 1600 is 8.5 hours.

steps.detail: 0730 to 1600 is 8.5 hours.
Regular peaked from 0930 to 1130. NPH peaks from 1130 to 1930.
Reduced intake at the peak sets up the low.

elimination.verdict: The Humulin N is still within its peak.

questions.stem: At 0730 a 63-year-old who is eating normally is due regular insulin 6 units and NPH 16 units in one syringe. His tray comes at 0800. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose before preparing the dose
options.rationale: The current value decides whether insulin is safe to give now.

options.text: Confirm the regular vial is clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is clear. A cloudy vial is not used.

options.text: Roll the NPH vial gently between the palms
options.rationale: NPH is a cloudy suspension that is rolled to mix it before drawing.

options.text: Draw the NPH first, then the regular to 22 units
options.rationale: The total is right but the order is wrong. Clear before cloudy keeps NPH out of the regular vial.

options.text: Give the dose now, 30 minutes before the tray
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so half an hour ahead matches it to the meal.

options.text: Massage the site after withdrawing the needle
options.rationale: Massage changes how fast the dose is absorbed.

questions.takeaway: Before a mixed dose: check the glucose, check each vial's appearance, roll the NPH, draw clear before cloudy to the total, time it 30 minutes before the meal.
questions.strategy: One wrong option has a correct number in it. Check the order of the draw as well as the total.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose check, clear vial, rolled NPH and timing are all correct.
22 units is the right total. NPH first is the wrong order.
It alters absorption.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and E.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with erratic glucose readings was taught site rotation last week. Which report at today's visit shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "I use my abdomen in the morning and my thigh at night."
options.rationale: Tempting because it sounds organized. Moving between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate.

options.text: "I use the exact same spot so the dose stays predictable."
options.rationale: One region is right, but one spot is not. Rotation within the region protects the tissue.

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and pick a different spot each time."
options.rationale: One anatomical region with rotation inside it keeps absorption consistent.

options.text: "I move from abdomen to arm to thigh through the week."
options.rationale: This is rotation between regions, which varies absorption dose to dose.

questions.takeaway: One region, a new spot within it each time. Rotating between regions changes absorption and makes readings erratic.
questions.strategy: Three options change something that should stay fixed or fix something that should change. Find the one that keeps the region and moves the spot.

steps.detail: Two options move between regions. They say the same thing.
It keeps the region but never rotates.
Same region, different spot.

elimination.verdict: Stays in the abdomen and picks a different spot each time.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes and influenza calls the clinic. She has taken her insulin and is sipping fluids often. Her glucose has stayed near 270 mg/dL since morning. What does the nurse tell her to do next?

options.text: Test for ketones
options.rationale: A glucose that stays over 240 during illness calls for a ketone test, which shows whether ketoacidosis is developing.

options.text: Keep sipping fluids and recheck in four hours
options.rationale: Tempting because both are sick day rules. She is already doing them. The sustained value over 240 adds a step.

options.text: Skip the next insulin dose until she can eat
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose. Stopping insulin leads to ketoacidosis.

options.text: Drink a glass of juice to keep her strength up
options.rationale: Her glucose is high. Fast-acting carbohydrate is for a low.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: keep taking insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, keep fluids going, test ketones when glucose stays over 240.
questions.strategy: Ask what the stem says she is already doing. The answer is the sick day rule she has not yet followed.

steps.detail: Insulin taken, fluids going.

steps.action: Find the trigger in the stem
steps.detail: Glucose staying over 240.

steps.action: Match the trigger to its rule
steps.detail: Over 240 means ketones.

elimination.verdict: Test for ketones.

questions.stem: At 0700 the nurse receives four fingerstick results at once. Which client does the nurse see first?

options.text: A 60-year-old at 212 mg/dL who reports thirst
options.rationale: Tempting because he has a symptom. Above 180 needs assessment and a review of orders, which can follow the low.

options.text: A 71-year-old at 164 mg/dL who is asking for breakfast
options.rationale: Within the 70 to 180 inpatient target.

options.text: A 55-year-old at 96 mg/dL who slept poorly
options.rationale: A normal value. Poor sleep is not a glucose problem.

options.text: A 67-year-old at 68 mg/dL who says he feels fine
options.rationale: Under 70 is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern, with or without symptoms.

questions.takeaway: A glucose under 70 is treated first, even in a client with no symptoms. A high with thirst is assessed next.
questions.strategy: Do not let the symptom pull you. Rank the numbers against 70 and 180 first.

steps.detail: 68 is low, 96 and 164 are in range, 212 is high.
A low can worsen in minutes. A high of 212 is assessed, not rushed.
Feeling fine does not make 68 safe.

elimination.verdict: The 67-year-old at 68 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old going home on regular 5 units and NPH 15 units in one syringe gives a return demonstration. Which sequence shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws NPH to 15, then regular to 20
options.rationale: Right total, wrong order. A syringe holding NPH should not enter the regular vial.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20
options.rationale: Clear before cloudy, with the second insulin drawn to the total of both doses.

options.text: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 15
options.rationale: Right order, but stopping at 15 gives only 10 units of NPH.

options.text: Rolls the regular, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20
options.rationale: The vial that needs rolling is the cloudy NPH. Drawing it unmixed gives an uneven dose.

questions.takeaway: Roll the NPH, draw regular first, then draw NPH to the total of both doses.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: which vial is rolled, which is drawn first, where the plunger stops.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH first is out.
5 plus 15 is 20, so stopping at 15 is out.
The cloudy vial is rolled.

elimination.verdict: Rolls the NPH, draws regular to 5, then NPH to 20.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with an insulin pump is admitted. Her glucose has climbed from 150 to 320 mg/dL in four hours with ketones present. Lunch was normal. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Have her deliver a correction dose through the pump
options.rationale: Tempting because the glucose is high. If the pump is not delivering, a dose sent through it will not reach her.

options.text: Ask what she ate for lunch
options.rationale: The stem already says lunch was normal. A meal does not explain ketones.

options.text: Inspect the infusion site and tubing
options.rationale: A fast rise with ketones in a pump user points to interrupted delivery, since there is no long-acting insulin on board.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Waiting lets ketones build in a client who may be getting no insulin.

questions.takeaway: A pump holds only rapid-acting insulin. Rising glucose with ketones means look for an interruption at the site or in the tubing first.
questions.strategy: Two options treat the high. Ask whether the route for that treatment can be trusted yet.

steps.detail: Fast rise plus ketones means no insulin is arriving.
Lunch was normal.

steps.action: Check the delivery before using it
steps.detail: A correction through a blocked line does nothing.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the infusion site and tubing.

questions.stem: At 1500 a 73-year-old who received NPH at 0700 has a fingerstick glucose of 56 mg/dL. He is alert, shaky and able to swallow. Place the nurse's actions in order.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: First. The glucose is known and under 70, so treatment comes before anything else.

options.text: Recheck the fingerstick glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck number, not how he feels, shows whether the low has resolved.

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g if the recheck is under 70
options.rationale: Treatment repeats until the glucose is at least 70.

options.text: Review his intake and insulin timing to find the cause
options.rationale: Once he is safe, work out why it happened. He is in the NPH peak.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still under 70, then work out why it happened.
questions.strategy: The assessment is already in the stem. Start with treatment and leave the search for a cause until he is above 70.

steps.detail: 56 mg/dL, alert, able to swallow.
No further assessment is needed to act.
Finding the reason does not raise his glucose.

elimination.verdict: Treat, recheck, repeat if needed, then find the cause.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old takes NPH each morning and metoprolol. At 1400 the nurse makes rounds. Which finding prompts an immediate glucose check?

options.text: New sweating with a heart rate of 66
options.rationale: Metoprolol blunts the fast heart rate of a low, but sweating usually persists. He is also in the NPH peak.

options.text: A heart rate of 62 with dry skin
options.rationale: An expected heart rate on metoprolol, with no sign of a low.

options.text: A request for water after walking in the hall
options.rationale: Thirst after activity is not a sign of hypoglycemia.

options.text: Dozing after lunch, fully alert when spoken to
options.rationale: An afternoon nap in a client who wakes fully alert is not a sign of a low.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask shakiness and tachycardia. Sweating usually remains, so it is the cue to check a glucose.
questions.strategy: Do not wait for tachycardia in a client on a beta blocker. Look for the sign the drug does not hide.

steps.detail: Metoprolol hides the fast heart rate.
1400 is 7 hours after morning NPH, inside its peak.
Sweating.

elimination.verdict: New sweating with a heart rate of 66.

questions.stem: The nurse gave a 65-year-old Humulin R 8 units at 1130 for a 1200 lunch. At 1200 the kitchen says trays will be 45 minutes late. He is alert with no symptoms. Which action is best?

options.text: Notify the provider that the tray is late
options.rationale: Tempting because a delay that affects the regimen is reported. Calling does not protect him from insulin that is already working.

options.text: Document the delay and check him at 1245
options.rationale: Regular insulin has started working. Waiting until the tray comes leaves him uncovered.

options.text: Give his next dose 45 minutes later
options.rationale: This addresses the next meal, not the insulin already given.

options.text: Check his glucose and get food to him now
options.rationale: Regular insulin starts in 30 to 60 minutes, so he needs food now and a glucose check while intake is delayed.

questions.takeaway: Insulin already given cannot wait for a late tray. Recheck the glucose and bring food to the client.
questions.strategy: The insulin is in. Pick the action that deals with this dose in this client right now.

steps.detail: Given at 1130, regular insulin is active by 1200.
Next dose and a 1245 check do not help now.
Food and a glucose check protect him first. The call can follow.

elimination.verdict: Check his glucose and get food to him now.

questions.stem: At 1100 a 59-year-old with a glucose of 248 mg/dL received correction insulin as ordered. Which finding at the follow-up check shows the treatment was effective?

options.text: He says he feels less thirsty
options.rationale: A symptom report is not the measure. The glucose value is.

options.text: His glucose is 192 mg/dL
options.rationale: Improved, but still above the 180 upper limit.

options.text: His glucose is 156 mg/dL
options.rationale: Within the 70 to 180 inpatient target range.

options.text: His glucose is 66 mg/dL
options.rationale: Under 70 is hypoglycemia, which is harm from the treatment.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands the value inside 70 to 180 mg/dL. Lower is not better once it passes 70.
questions.strategy: Lowest is not the goal. Place each number against the target range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 192 is still high. 66 is a low.

steps.action: Prefer the number to the symptom
steps.detail: Glucose is evaluated by glucose.

elimination.verdict: His glucose is 156 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old who takes glipizide each morning is fasting for a 1000 procedure. His 0700 glucose is 88 mg/dL and the dose is due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the glipizide, since it is not insulin
options.rationale: Tempting because many oral drugs do not cause lows. A sulfonylurea forces insulin release whether or not he eats.

options.text: Hold the dose and clarify the order with the provider
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea with no food can cause a low, so the dose is questioned before it is given.

options.text: Give the glipizide with a glass of juice
options.rationale: He is fasting for the procedure. His glucose is not low.

options.text: Give half the dose and recheck at 0900
options.rationale: Changing a dose is outside the nurse's scope.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide, glyburide and glimepiride cause lows when a meal is skipped. Question the dose for a fasting client.
questions.strategy: Ask what this drug does when there is no food. Then stay inside nursing scope.

steps.detail: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea.
A nurse does not halve a dose.
It breaks the fast and treats a low he does not have.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and clarify the order with the provider.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old on bedtime NPH has had a 0700 glucose over 230 mg/dL for three mornings. No overnight values are recorded. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the provider for a 0300 glucose check
options.rationale: A morning high can follow an overnight low or rise with no low. The 0200 to 0300 value tells them apart.

options.text: Ask the provider to increase the bedtime NPH
options.rationale: Tempting because the morning value is high. If an overnight low is causing a rebound, more insulin makes the low worse.

options.text: Hold tonight's bedtime NPH
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not held without an order. Holding it guesses at the cause.

options.text: Give his breakfast 30 minutes earlier
options.rationale: Meal timing does not explain or correct a fasting high.

questions.takeaway: A repeated morning high needs an overnight value before the insulin is changed. Somogyi is a low that rebounds. Dawn rises without a low.
questions.strategy: Two options change the insulin in opposite directions. When both are guesses, pick the option that gets the missing data.

steps.detail: No overnight values.
Increase and hold both assume a cause.
A 0300 check decides which way to go.

elimination.verdict: Ask the provider for a 0300 glucose check.

questions.scenario: A 60-year-old is going home on Lantus at bedtime and Humalog with meals. The nurse evaluates his statements after teaching.
questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether the teaching was understood or needs reinforcement.

rows.text: "I take the Humalog when my plate is in front of me."
rows.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin starts in 10 to 30 minutes, so it is given with the food.

rows.text: "If I skip dinner, I skip my Lantus that night too."
rows.rationale: Lantus is basal insulin with no pronounced peak. It is not matched to meals.

rows.text: "If my Lantus looks cloudy, I roll it before drawing."
rows.rationale: Glargine is clear. A cloudy vial is discarded. Only NPH is rolled.

rows.text: "If my sugar is 62, I take glucose and check again in 15 minutes."
rows.rationale: Under 70 is treated with fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecked in 15 minutes.

rows.text: "I rub the spot after the shot so it works faster."
rows.rationale: Massage changes absorption and can make readings erratic.

questions.takeaway: Humalog follows food. Lantus does not. Lantus is clear. Sites are not massaged. A low is treated and rechecked in 15 minutes.
questions.strategy: Judge each statement alone. Watch for a correct NPH habit applied to the wrong insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mealtime insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not.
Rolling belongs to NPH only.
No massage after injection.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 and 4 are understood. Rows 2, 3 and 5 need reinforcement.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old jogs after dinner and takes regular insulin before that meal. He has had two evening lows this week after injecting his thigh. Which plan does the nurse suggest for the dinner dose?

options.text: Keep the thigh and inject deeper
options.rationale: Depth is not the issue. The working muscle speeds absorption.

options.text: Use the thigh and massage it before the jog
options.rationale: Massage and exercise both speed absorption, which would add to the lows.

options.text: Inject the abdomen at dinner
options.rationale: The abdomen is not the working limb during a jog, so absorption is not sped by the exercise.

options.text: Skip the dinner dose on jogging days
options.rationale: Tempting because it stops the low. Omitting a prescribed dose is not the nurse's or client's call. The site is the cause.

questions.takeaway: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb. Do not inject a limb that is about to work.
questions.strategy: The lows have a pattern in the stem: thigh plus jog. Change the site, not the prescription.

steps.detail: Lows follow thigh injections before a jog.
Massage and a working thigh.
Skipping a dose is not a site fix.

elimination.verdict: Inject the abdomen at dinner.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old had a 0300 glucose of 46 mg/dL followed by a 0700 glucose of 250 mg/dL, so the provider lowered her bedtime NPH. Which result shows the change was effective?

options.text: 0700 glucose 122 mg/dL, no overnight check done
options.rationale: Tempting because the morning value is in range. Without the 0300 value the overnight low could still be there.

options.text: 0300 glucose 58 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 204 mg/dL
options.rationale: Both improved slightly, but she is still low overnight and still rebounding.

options.text: 0300 glucose 52 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 148 mg/dL
options.rationale: The morning value is in range, but the overnight value is still a low.

options.text: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL
options.rationale: The overnight low is gone and the morning value is in range, so the rebound has stopped.

questions.takeaway: The problem was the overnight low. The change worked only when the 0300 value is above 70 and the morning value is in range.
questions.strategy: Evaluate the problem that was treated. The dose was lowered to stop a 0300 low, so the 0300 value must be in the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A low at 0300 that rebounded.

steps.action: Cut any option with a 0300 value under 70
steps.detail: 52 and 58 are still lows.

steps.action: Cut the option with no 0300 value
steps.detail: It cannot show the low is gone.

elimination.verdict: 0300 glucose 102 mg/dL, 0700 glucose 136 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomited twice and refuses dinner. Her glucose is 228 mg/dL. Lantus 20 units and Humalog 5 units with the meal are both due. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Hold both insulins and notify the provider
options.rationale: Tempting because she is not eating. Basal insulin is not matched to food and is not held without an order.

options.text: Give the Lantus, hold the Humalog and notify the provider
options.rationale: Basal insulin continues during illness. Mealtime insulin follows food, so it is held and her intake is reported.

options.text: Give both insulins as scheduled
options.rationale: Humalog with no meal sets up a low.

options.text: Give the Humalog only, to bring the glucose down
options.rationale: Humalog here is ordered for the meal. Using it as a correction dose is not what the order says.

questions.takeaway: No food means no mealtime insulin. Basal insulin still goes in, especially in illness and type 1 diabetes.
questions.strategy: Treat the two insulins as two separate decisions. Ask of each one: is it matched to food?

steps.detail: No meal, so hold it and report.
Not timed to food. Illness raises glucose.
Give one, hold one.

elimination.verdict: Give the Lantus, hold the Humalog and notify the provider.

questions.stem: At 1015 a 72-year-old who received Humulin R at 0730 and ate little breakfast snaps at the nurse and refuses his bath. He is awake and answering questions. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Check his fingerstick glucose
options.rationale: New irritability at the peak of regular insulin after a small meal suggests a low. The check takes seconds and directs treatment.

options.text: Give 4 ounces of juice
options.rationale: Tempting because a low is likely. He is awake and stable enough for a quick check. The value has not been measured.

options.text: Return in an hour to offer the bath again
options.rationale: This treats a behavior change in a client on insulin as a mood problem.

options.text: Ask the provider about a sleep aid
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem points to a sleep problem.

questions.takeaway: A behavior change in a client on insulin is a glucose check first, most of all at the insulin's peak with reduced intake.
questions.strategy: No glucose value is in the stem. When the assessment is missing and the client is awake, get the number before you treat.

steps.detail: 0730 to 1015 is inside the 2 to 4 hour peak.
None is given.
A fingerstick is fast and tells you whether juice is needed.

elimination.verdict: Check his fingerstick glucose.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes has influenza and cannot keep food down. Her glucose is 190 mg/dL. Which statement shows the sick day teaching needs to be repeated?

options.text: "I will skip my Lantus until I can eat again."
options.rationale: Basal insulin is not matched to food and is never stopped on sick days. This is the statement that needs correcting.

options.text: "I will hold my Humalog when I cannot eat a meal."
options.rationale: Sounds like skipping insulin, which tempts. Mealtime insulin follows food, so holding it without a meal is correct.

options.text: "I will test for ketones if I stay over 240."
options.rationale: Correct sick day rule.

options.text: "I will check my glucose every four hours tonight."
options.rationale: Correct. Glucose is checked every three to four hours during illness.

questions.takeaway: Rapid acting insulin follows food. Basal insulin does not, and it continues through illness.
questions.strategy: Two statements involve holding insulin. Sort them by which insulin depends on a meal.

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Ketones over 240 and checks every three to four hours are right.
Humalog follows food. Lantus does not.

elimination.verdict: Skipping the Lantus is the error.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old's glucose readings are still erratic two weeks after site teaching. Which report best explains the readings?

options.text: "I stay in my abdomen and use a new spot each time."
options.rationale: Correct rotation within one region. It keeps absorption steady.

options.text: "I pinch the skin and go straight in at 90 degrees."
options.rationale: Correct technique.

options.text: "I rub the spot afterward so it will not bruise."
options.rationale: Massaging the site changes how fast the insulin is absorbed, which makes the readings swing.

options.text: "I skip the bruised spot from last week's injection."
options.rationale: Correct. Bruised tissue is avoided.

questions.takeaway: Do not massage an insulin site. Rubbing changes absorption even when the rotation is correct.
questions.strategy: The rotation sounds fixed. Look for the other habit that changes absorption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One region, new spot. Correct.
Pinch and 90 degrees. Correct.
Rubbing the site.

elimination.verdict: Rubbing the site explains the swings.

questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse reviews four clients. Which client does the nurse check first?

options.text: Humulin R at 0730, ate all of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because regular insulin is at its peak. A full breakfast and no symptoms make a low less likely.

options.text: Lantus at 0800, ate 25% of breakfast, no symptoms
options.rationale: Tempting because of the poor intake. Lantus has no pronounced peak and is not matched to meals.

options.text: Humalog with breakfast, glucose 240 mg/dL, reports thirst
options.rationale: A high with thirst is assessed next, after a possible low.

options.text: Glipizide and metoprolol at 0800, skipped breakfast, new sweating
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea with a skipped meal causes a low. The beta blocker hides shakiness and a fast heart rate, so sweating is the only warning.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas cause lows when a meal is skipped. Beta blockers mask the warning signs, and sweating usually remains.
questions.strategy: Each client has a risk on paper. Find the one who has a symptom, then work out what it means.

steps.detail: A high with thirst follows a possible low.
One ate fully at the peak. One has an insulin with no peak.
Sweating with a skipped meal on glipizide and metoprolol.

elimination.verdict: The sweating client on glipizide and metoprolol.

questions.stem: A client on bedtime NPH has a 0300 glucose of 148 mg/dL and a 0700 glucose of 240 mg/dL. A coworker suggests asking the provider to lower the bedtime NPH. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree and request a lower bedtime NPH dose
options.rationale: Tempting because a lower dose fixes a rebound high. A rebound needs an overnight low, and 148 is not low.

options.text: Report both values and that no overnight low occurred
options.rationale: The glucose rose without a low, which is the dawn pattern. The provider needs both values to choose the change.

options.text: Ask for another 0300 check before reporting anything
options.rationale: The overnight value is already in hand. Repeating it delays the report.

options.text: Give a bedtime snack tonight and recheck at 0700
options.rationale: A snack treats an overnight low that did not happen and would raise the morning value.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi is an overnight low that rebounds to a morning high. Dawn rises without a low. The 0300 value tells them apart.
questions.strategy: Decide what the 0300 number rules out before you choose what to ask for.

steps.detail: 148 is not a low.
A rise without a low is dawn, so lowering the dose does not fit.
The needed assessment is already done.

elimination.verdict: Report both values. There was no overnight low.

questions.stem: At 1100 a client with a glucose of 262 mg/dL received correction insulin. At 1300 his glucose is 66 mg/dL. He feels fine and says, "Finally, it is down." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: 66 is under 70, so it is treated now even without symptoms. The correction went too far.

options.text: Document the result as an effective treatment
options.rationale: Tempting because the number fell and he feels well. Effective means 70 to 180, and lower is not better.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before acting
options.rationale: Tempting because a recheck is part of the rule. The recheck comes after the carbohydrate.

options.text: Hold his next mealtime insulin and notify the provider
options.rationale: Reporting the low is reasonable later. It does not raise his glucose now.

questions.takeaway: Effective glucose treatment lands between 70 and 180 mg/dL. Under 70 is treated first, with or without symptoms.
questions.strategy: The number moved the right way. Check where it stopped.

steps.detail: 66 is below the 70 line.
No symptoms does not cancel the rule.
Treat, then recheck, then report.

elimination.verdict: Treat the low with fast-acting carbohydrate.
